new_statements.quote: [p. 556, Baria:] Woordvorm en klemtoon zijn als in 't Barée. [p. 540, Groep I (Barée):] Stammen meest tweelettergrepig, klemtoon op de voorlaatste. Alleen de suffixen -a en -aka doen den klemtoon verspringen naar de voorlaatste van het daarmee samengesteld woord. Andere suffixen brengen den klemtoon niet van zijne plaats. [p. 557:] In het Parigi'sch is deze e los van het voorgaande woord, in 't Baria en Barée niet, daar zij den klemtoon verplaatst naar de haar voorafgaande lettergreep. Bv. Baria: alutáe, het hout, Bar. ajuta; tadojáe, de huig.
new_statements.translation: [p. 556, Baria:] Word shape and stress are as in Bare'e. [p. 540, Group I (Bare'e):] Stems mostly disyllabic, stress on the penultimate syllable. Only the suffixes -a and -aka make the stress jump to the penult of the word so formed. Other suffixes do not move the stress from its place. [p. 557:] In Parigi this e [the article] is detached from the preceding word, in Baria and Bare'e it is not, since it shifts the stress onto the syllable preceding it. E.g. Baria: alutáe 'the wood', Bare'e ajuta; tadojáe 'the uvula'.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the (mostly disyllabic) stem; suffixes -a and -aka re-place stress on the new penult, while other suffixes leave stress on the stem's penult; the enclitic article -e attracts stress to the syllable immediately before it (alutá-e).
new_statements.exceptions: Stress stays on the stem penult under most suffixes (so it can be antepenultimate in the suffixed word); only -a and -aka re-locate it to the derived word's penult; the enclitic article e makes stress fall on the preceding syllable. Adriani also notes that Tawaili (a Palu-bay Kaili variety, distinct from Tawaelia) and Palu shift stress with every suffix (p. 565).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level; stated by comparison ('as in Bare'e') within a survey overview whose Baria data were gathered without on-site work (p. 554: 'Een onderzoek ter plaatse ligt voorloopig nog buiten ons bereik'); the language is called 'Baria' after its negator ba-ria and located in Tawaelia, the upland of the Tambarana.
new_statements.identity_note: The source calls the language "Baria" (named after its negator ba-ria) and locates it in Tawaelia, the upland of the Tambarana river (p. 554); Tawaelia/Baria/Topobaria are the alternate names of Sedoa [sedo1237, ISO tvw] on sulang.org, which cites this same passage (Adriani 1898:554) for Sedoa's location. Adriani did not visit the area; his Baria data came from reports and displaced To Palapi speakers. Not to be confused with "Tawaili'sch" (Tawaeli on Palu Bay, a Ledo/Kaili variety) discussed on pp. 564-565 of the same overview.

sources.note: p. 556 (Baria section): 'Woordvorm en klemtoon zijn als in 't Barée'; the Bare'e (Group I) rule on p. 540: stems mostly disyllabic, stress on the penult; only suffixes -a and -aka shift stress to the new penult, other suffixes leave it in place; Group II (Parigi type, to which Baria belongs grammatically) 'Woordvorm en Klemtoon als in 't Barée' (p. 542); p. 557: in Baria (and Bare'e) the enclitic article e draws the stress onto the syllable before it, e.g. alutáe 'the wood', tadojáe 'the uvula'. Adriani adds (p. 554) that on-site investigation of Baria was still out of reach.
